A Decision at Every Pixel

Five test photos from the lecture's notebook, and what five methods say about every pixel: person or background. Three of them are the notebook's networks, which share Lecture 15's ResNet-18 and differ only in how they return to full size. Move over a picture to read the probability at one pixel, move the threshold, and watch pixel accuracy and IoU disagree.

Accuracy flatters
Press "call everything background". Pixel accuracy stays high, because most pixels are background, and IoU drops to 0. IoU only counts the pixels that the prediction or the truth call person (green, orange and blue), so the easy background cannot pad the score.

    
What the skips buy
Switch between coarse, decoder and U-Net on the same photo. All three know where the people are. The orange and blue pixels sit on the outlines, and they thin out as the network gets higher-resolution information: legs separate, and gaps between arms and bodies open.

    
Labels are decisions
On the photo with the cyclist, the hand-drawn mask marks only the walker: the dataset labels pedestrians. Every method that marks the cyclist as a person is charged for it in orange. A score measures agreement with somebody's labels.

    
Blobs are not people
The readout counts the connected blobs of the mask. On the photo where pedestrians overlap, every pixel can be right while the count is wrong: semantic segmentation labels pixels and does not tell objects apart.
